newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.N. chief launches chemical weapons watchdog. [CORRECTED 11:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief launches chemical weapons watchdog. [CORRECTED 11:15 GMT]

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan opened the inaugural conference on Tuesday (corrects day) of a new agency charged with enforcing a global ban on chemical weapons.
Attended by 160 countries, the conference is being held one week after the treaty banning the development, production, stockpiling and use of chemical weapons came into force.
The treaty has been hailed as the most ambitious disarmament agreement ever because it seeks to eliminate an entire class of weapons and includes unprecedented verification measures.

The United States secured the right to vote at the first conference of the new Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) when its Senate ratified the treaty on just days before it entered force on April 29.
A total of 88 countries now have ratified the treaty and will be able to vote on key matters such as a budget and a director general to run the OPCW from its offices in The Hague.
The three-week conference will also elect a 41-member executive council to supervise the new agency's work and discuss the fine detail of its verification and enforcement tasks.
A further 77 countries have signed the treaty but not yet ratified it and, while they may attend the conference, they are not allowed to vote or be elected to the executive committee.

These countries include Russia, where parliament has postponed approval of the treaty until later this year despite pressure from President Boris Yeltsin, arguing Russia needs more time and Western financial aid to destroy its chemical weapons.

Russia and the United States are the two biggest holders of chemical weapons, with combined stocks of 70,000 tonnes, and diplomats involved in setting up the OPCW had originally hoped to get both countries on board before the ban entered force.
In fact both countries almost missed the boat, with Senate hawks threatening to block U.S. ratification, which eventually came just five days before the ban took effect.
In his opening speech, Annan said the chemical weapons treaty and the setting up of the OPCW was "a momentous act of peace".
"One of the most monstrous tools of warfare has been ruled intolerable..." he said.
But he urged those countries who had still not signed and ratified the treaty to do so quickly to make it truly universal.
Chemical weapons were used to devastating effect in World War One when chlorine and mustard gas claimed 100,000 lives.
More recently Iraq used mustard gas against Iran in the 1980s and in March 1995 a Japanese sect used sarin nerve gas to attack commuters on Tokyo's underground rail system.
Chemical weapons have long been condemned as cruel and indiscriminate but it was not until 1992 that a comprehensive ban could be negotiated.
The OPCW is currently training a force of 140 inspectors for its core task of monitoring compliance with the treaty.
Member states must destroy their chemical weapons within 10 years and provide detailed information about the production and export of listed chemicals used to make such weapons.
They are barred from supplying listed chemicals to non-members and must open their chemical plants to the OPCW both for routine and short-notice challenge inspections.
Any member state which suspects a treaty violation can call for a challenge inspection, which can only be blocked if at least three-quarters of the executive council votes against it.
If an inspection confirms a violation, the offending country faces expulsion from the OPCW and possible U.N. sanctions.
Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok told the conference this extensive verification regime meant the OPCW could bite as well as bark.

Countries which remain outside the treaty -- such as Iraq, Libya, North Korea and Syria -- are not only conspicuous by their absence but could also face problems obtaining listed chemicals needed by their industries for legitimate purposes.
Many of the so-called precursors used to make chemical weapons also have mundane, non-lethal uses in products such as medicines, dyes and weed-killers.
Even staunch advocates of the chemical weapons treaty admit its verification system can never be 100 percent watertight, but they insist it is tough enough to deter and isolate cheats.
The OPCW estimates that a budget of some $50 million is needed for 1997, its first year of operation, and so far it has been operating on advance contributions from member states.
A spokesman said the OPCW faced no immediate cash problems and was optimistic an adequate budget would be approved.
